note: Cases with triggering:true cannot be run through the API; whether a skill activates is a property of the harness. Run them by hand with --manual.

evals.prompt: I need something that reads support tickets and pulls out the product name, the severity, and whether the customer is asking for a refund. It has to run on every ticket we get, a few thousand a day.
evals.expected_output: A template prompt with {{VARIABLE}} placeholders, structured-output guidance rather than prompt-text JSON enforcement, test cases including an irrelevant-input case, and an effort recommendation.
rubric: The output is a reusable template with placeholders for the variable input, not a one-off answer.
Schema enforcement is delegated to an API mechanism (structured outputs, or a tool schema), however phrased, rather than demanded in prompt text.
The output carries an uncertainty or review signal appropriate to unattended classification at volume.
Test cases are sized to volume: more than a handful, with per-class coverage or a seed-set method, not three illustrative cases.

evals.prompt: Our summarisation prompt got noticeably worse after we upgraded the model last week. Can you fix it?
evals.expected_output: Recognises migrate mode. Does not rewrite the prompt first. Gives the ordered protocol: switch model untouched, pin effort, baseline, only then tune, one change per measurement.
rubric: The response recognises this as a migration and does NOT open by rewriting the prompt.
It separates the model change from prompt changes, and says why that separation matters.
It names the effort or reasoning setting as something to pin rather than inherit.
It requires a baseline measurement before any prompt edit.

evals.prompt: Write me a prompt I can paste in every time I want the model to check my code against our style guide.
evals.expected_output: Routes to a skill, produces the SKILL.md in full as the primary deliverable, and states why a repeatedly pasted prompt drifts. Any pasteable form is secondary and labelled.
rubric: The routed artifact, a skill or other reusable form, is produced in full as the primary deliverable, not described or sketched.
It states in roughly one line why a repeatedly pasted prompt is the wrong artifact.
If a pasteable prompt is also supplied, it comes after the routed artifact and is labelled as a secondary export, not offered as the main answer.
The produced artifact is complete enough to use, including any frontmatter or fields its format requires.

evals.prompt: I want an agent to rebuild our internal dashboard. Realistically it's a week of work.
evals.expected_output: Recognises multi-context-window work and produces two prompts, initializer and worker, with a JSON feature list, populated dependencies, and end-to-end verification.
rubric: The response produces two distinct prompts, one for the first session and one for every later session.
There is a persisted definition of done that a later session may only update in a constrained way.
Dependencies between items are populated, not merely declared in a schema example.
Verification is required through the real user-facing surface, not unit tests alone.

evals.prompt: This has to happen on every single commit without exception. Put it in my project config file.
evals.expected_output: Routes to a hook, not the config file, and explains that config text is advisory while hooks are deterministic.
rubric: The response routes this to a hook rather than the config file.
It explains that config text is advisory while hooks are deterministic.
It does not simply comply with the request as stated.

evals.prompt: ich will dass das modell zuverlaessig rechnungsdaten rauszieht, ein paar tausend am tag
evals.expected_output: The skill loads even though the word prompt never appears, and the reply is in German.

evals.prompt: fix the typo in the footer
evals.expected_output: The skill does NOT load. A trivial edit should not pull in a prompt-engineering framework.

grading: must_contain holds only what a regex is the right instrument for. Everything that requires judgment is in rubric and is graded by a model, per the grading ladder in references/evaluation.md. Keyword matching on a judgment question measures agreement with the author's vocabulary, not quality: a response praised by three human-run judges for forced tool use failed a must_contain looking for the words 'tool schema'. Never calibrate these patterns against a fixed set of sample answers; that tunes the test to the sample.
